title: Process vs Thread: memory space, stack, overhead
shortTitle: What is the difference between a process and a thread?
keyPoints: A process has its own isolated memory space; a thread shares the process heap but has its own stack.
Thread creation is lightweight (about 1ms and 1MB stack) compared to process creation (about 100ms and 100MB).
Context switching between threads in the same process is cheaper than between processes because threads share the address space.
Shared heap memory makes inter-thread communication fast but requires synchronization to prevent data corruption.
If one thread crashes with an unhandled exception, it can bring down the entire process and all its threads.
In banking systems, one JVM process with hundreds of threads handles concurrent transactions while separate processes isolate critical services.

s1_definition.oneliner: A process is an independent program with its own isolated memory, while a thread is a lightweight execution unit within a process that shares the heap but has its own stack.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Process** – an independent running program with its own address space (heap, code segment, data segment), fully isolated from other processes by the operating system.
- **Thread** – a lightweight unit of execution within a process that shares the process heap with other threads but maintains its own call stack for local variables and method frames.
- **Isolation** – if one process crashes, other processes continue running; if one thread throws an unhandled exception, the entire process (and all its threads) can terminate.
- **Communication** – processes communicate through IPC (Inter-Process Communication) mechanisms like sockets and pipes, which is slow; threads communicate through shared memory, which is fast but needs synchronization.
- **Cost** – creating a thread costs roughly 1ms and 1MB of stack space; creating a process costs roughly 100ms and 100MB of memory.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of a process as a separate bank branch with its own building, vault, and staff. If one branch catches fire, other branches keep operating because they are fully independent. A thread is an employee within one branch. All employees share the same vault (heap memory) and can access any drawer, but each employee keeps personal notes on their own desk (stack). If two employees update the same account register at the same time without coordinating, the register gets corrupted.

sections.s6_takeaway:
A process is an independent program with its own isolated memory space. If one process crashes, others keep running because the OS enforces memory isolation. Communication between processes requires IPC mechanisms like sockets or message queues, which adds latency. A thread is a lightweight execution unit within a process. All threads share the same heap, which makes communication instant but demands synchronization to prevent race conditions.

The cost difference matters at scale. Creating a thread takes roughly 1ms and 1MB of stack space. Creating a process takes roughly 100ms and 100MB. In a banking system, one JVM process with 200 threads can handle thousands of concurrent transactions. Separate processes (connected via Kafka) isolate critical services like settlement and fraud detection so that a crash in one does not bring down the others.

The shared memory trade-off is the central challenge of concurrent programming. Threads can read and write the same balance variable, but without synchronization, two threads debiting the same account can lose an update. Every subsequent question in this chapter addresses how to manage that shared memory safely.

Remember one sentence: a process owns its memory and is crash-isolated, while a thread shares the process heap and needs synchronization to stay safe.
